content: The burden of asthma on both patients and healthcare systems is significant. To address challenges in asthma management, chronic disease management programmes have been developed. These programmes go beyond simple patient education and consist of a coordinated set of interventions tailored to the needs of patients. They emphasize the integration of healthcare services provided by multiple professionals, promote patient self-management, and include educational components. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of chronic disease management programmes for adults with asthma. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO, up to June 2014. Additionally, selected journals were hand-searched, and reference lists of relevant reviews were examined. The review included individual or cluster-randomized controlled trials, non-randomized controlled trials, and controlled before-and-after studies. These studies compared chronic disease management programmes with usual care in adults aged 16 years or older who had a diagnosis of asthma. To qualify, the programmes had to meet at least five criteria: they needed to include an organizational component targeting patients, an organizational component targeting healthcare professionals or the healthcare system (or both), patient education or self-management support (or both), active involvement of at least two healthcare professionals in patient care, and a minimum duration of three months. Two independent reviewers screened the studies for eligibility and quality, extracted data, and contacted study authors for missing information when necessary. The results were pooled using a random-effects model, and the pooled mean or standardized mean differences (SMDs) were reported. A total of 20 studies involving 81,746 patients were included in the review. The median number of participants per study was 129.5, and follow-up periods ranged from 3 months to over 12 months. The mean age of participants was 42.5 years, 60% were female, and most had moderate to severe asthma. The methodological quality of the studies was moderate to low due to design limitations and wide confidence intervals for some outcomes. Compared to usual care, chronic disease management programmes led to improvements in asthma-specific quality of life (SMD 0.22, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.37), asthma severity scores (SMD 0.18, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.30), and lung function tests (SMD 0.19, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.30). However, the evidence for improvements in self-efficacy scores was inconclusive (SMD 0.51, 95% CI -0.08 to 1.11). Data on hospitalizations and emergency department or unscheduled visits were too heterogeneous to combine in a meta-analysis, and individual study results were inconclusive. Only a small number of studies reported on outcomes such as asthma exacerbations, days off work or school, use of an action plan, and patient satisfaction, and meta-analyses could not be performed for these outcomes. In conclusion, there is moderate to low-quality evidence that chronic disease management programmes for adults with asthma can improve asthma-specific quality of life, asthma severity, and lung function. These findings suggest that such programmes may be effective when compared to usual care. However, further research is needed to determine the optimal components of these programmes and their added value compared to education or self-management alone, which are typically offered to patients with asthma.
